title: The Oven of Akhnai
text:
The Babylonian Talmud tells of a debate among the sages over a clay oven built in separate rings with sand between them. Was it subject to the laws of ritual impurity? Rabbi Eliezer said it was not. All the other sages disagreed.

Rabbi Eliezer brought every argument he could, and they did not accept them. So he said: if the law is as I say, let this carob tree prove it. The carob tree uprooted itself and moved a hundred cubits. The sages said one does not bring proof from a carob tree. Let the stream prove it, he said, and the water flowed backward. Let the walls of the study house prove it, and the walls began to lean. Rabbi Yehoshua rebuked the walls, and out of respect for him they did not fall, and out of respect for Rabbi Eliezer they did not straighten. They are still leaning, the Talmud says.

Finally Rabbi Eliezer called on heaven itself, and a heavenly voice declared that the law was as he said. Rabbi Yehoshua stood up and quoted Deuteronomy: "It is not in heaven." The Torah had been given to people, and the law follows the majority.

The Talmud adds that the prophet Elijah later reported God's reaction: God smiled and said, "My children have defeated me." The sages then ruled against Rabbi Eliezer and placed him under a ban.
lesson: A group that agrees on how decisions are made must hold to that process, even when someone has a striking argument from outside it. And winning a vote does not excuse wounding a colleague.
people: Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah, the sages
date: Late 1st to early 2nd century (set); text c. 6th century
